subject: forensic-medicine
title: Bumper Fractures, Impact Phases and Run Over Injuries

steps.title: Three phases of pedestrian injury
steps.tx: Pedestrian impacts unfold in **three impact phases**. Primary impact injuries mark the first part struck by the vehicle. Secondary impact injuries follow as the vehicle throws or carries the body against its own parts, such as the bonnet and windscreen. Secondary or tertiary injuries arise when the victim strikes the ground or other objects. Diagramming the location, nature and extent of every injury reconstructs which phase produced it.
steps.say: First the vehicle strikes, then its bodywork strikes again, then the ground strikes, and each phase leaves its own injury set.

steps.title: The bumper fracture of the tibia
steps.tx: The signature primary injury is the **bumper fracture**, usually of the tibia, where the struck fragment displaces forward. The fracture is typically spiral or wedge shaped: the base of the triangular fragment marks the site of impact, and its apex points in the direction the vehicle was travelling. If the leg was lifted, the fracture is often transverse instead. In children the bumper reaches higher and usually fractures the femur.
steps.say: A wedge fracture of the tibia points its apex along the vehicle's travel, while children take the bumper on the femur.

steps.tx: On a tibial radiograph the primary impact often appears as a wedge. A **bumper fracture** usually sits in the tibia, and the struck fragment is driven forward. The triangular piece has its base at the impact site and its apex aimed along the vehicle's direction of travel. A lifted leg more often breaks transversely. In a child the bumper rides higher, so the femur is the bone that usually snaps.

steps.title: Reading walking from bumper levels
steps.tx: Details of level refine the story under **bumper height interpretation**. Braking dips the vehicle front, so injuries land lower than the static bumper height. Bumper fractures at different levels on the two legs, or present on one leg only, suggest the victim was walking or running, with the fracture higher in the leg that was planted on the ground. A sideways oriented victim shows fracture in one leg alone.
steps.say: Unequal bumper levels mean unequal leg positions, so a walking victim's planted leg takes the higher fracture.

steps.title: Secondary impact on bonnet and windscreen
steps.tx: After the leg strike, the body wraps onto the car in **secondary impact injuries**. If the foot stays fixed, the buttocks and back meet the bonnet and the spine can fracture dislocate, sometimes transecting cord and thoracic aorta. Falling on the hood can shear skin and fat off the thigh and buttock muscle into a pocket that fills with blood invisibly. Head strike on the windscreen adds skull and facial fractures.
steps.say: The body wraps onto bonnet and windscreen next, shearing thigh pockets and fracturing spine, ribs and skull.

steps.title: Rear impact and run over patterns
steps.tx: Struck from behind, a pedestrian shows **parallel linear tears of the abdomen and groin** from overstretching of skin, dry, yellow and bloodless, with cervical spine fracture or dislocation at the skull base from whiplash. Run over adds the crushing weight of the wheel: skin overstretches and splits, internal organs rupture under direct pressure, and a tyre tread patterned abrasion may print across the back, tying the vehicle to the body.
steps.say: Rear strikes tear groin skin in dry parallel lines and whip the neck, while run over crushes organs and prints the tyre.

steps.tx: A pedestrian hit from behind may show dry, yellow, bloodless splits of abdominal and groin skin from overstretching, plus neck injury where the spine meets the skull, from whiplash. When a wheel then passes over the body, crushing adds organ rupture under direct pressure and skin that splits as it is stretched. A **tyre tread patterned abrasion** can print across the back and link that vehicle to the victim.

steps.title: Speed decides the body trajectory
steps.tx: Vehicle speed writes the trajectory in **speed dependent pedestrian trajectories**. At twenty kilometres per hour the person is simply thrown away. At forty to fifty, a strike below the centre of gravity scoops the victim up onto the bonnet, injuring elbows, shoulders and head, before sliding off sideways. At eighty to one hundred the pedestrian is thrown higher, may strike the roof, somersault, and land on the road behind the car.
steps.say: Twenty throws aside, fifty scoops onto the bonnet, and a hundred can somersault the victim clean over the roof.

steps.title: Children and high fronted vehicles
steps.tx: Geometry changes everything for small victims in **child pedestrian impacts**. A car's front strikes a child above the centre of gravity, so the child is pushed down and run over rather than scooped up. Bumper fractures hit the femur, not the tibia. A fast bus, truck or van with a straight high front strikes an adult at hip or shoulder level and pushes the body forward in front of the vehicle, where it may then be run over on stopping.
steps.say: Children are knocked down and run over because the bumper meets them above their centre of gravity, at the femur.

steps.title: Waddell triad in child pedestrians
steps.tx: The classic child pattern taught for examinations is the **Waddell triad**: a femoral fracture from the bumper strike, an intrathoracic or intra abdominal injury as the chest or abdomen meets the vehicle front, and a head injury as the head strikes vehicle or ground. Finding all three in a child should immediately suggest a pedestrian vehicle impact and prompt a search for the tyre or grille pattern that identifies the vehicle class.
steps.say: Femur fracture plus chest or abdominal injury plus head injury is the Waddell triad of the child pedestrian.

steps.title: Occupant injuries and the second collision
steps.tx: Inside the vehicle, the **second collision** injures occupants when their bodies strike interior structures after the vehicle itself hits a barrier. Dashboard and windscreen impacts fracture the face and skull, and the most extensive fractures come from a head striking a flat surface. In pedestrians the head is injured twice, once by the vehicle and once by the road, so skull fractures involve almost all parts of the skull, especially the base.
steps.say: Occupants are injured by the second collision inside the car, and pedestrian heads are struck by both vehicle and road.
